# Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-0.6B-Base — LiteRT

[Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-0.6B-Base](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-0.6B-Base) (Apache-2.0) converted to LiteRT (.tflite) for fully on-device text-to-speech with 3-second voice cloning, in 10 languages at 24 kHz.

Qwen3-TTS is a speech LM: a Qwen3-style talker predicts 12.5 Hz frames of 16 codec tokens (first codebook by the talker, 15 residual codebooks by an inner "MTP" transformer), and a neural codec decoder renders PCM. LiteRT-LM's Engine decode loop does not support this generation structure yet, so the model runs as **three LiteRT graphs driven by a host-side loop** (LiteRT Compiled Model pattern). A complete Python reference pipeline and all conversion scripts live in the litert-samples sample: [`compiled_model_api/text_to_speech_lm`](https://github.com/john-rocky/litert-samples/tree/qwen3-tts-sample/compiled_model_api/text_to_speech_lm).

## Quick start (Python, desktop)

```bash
git clone -b qwen3-tts-sample https://github.com/john-rocky/litert-samples.git
cd litert-samples/compiled_model_api/text_to_speech_lm/python
pip install -r requirements.txt
python synthesize.py --text "Hello from LiteRT running fully on device." --output hello.wav
```

The script downloads this repository automatically (~1.4 GB for the default int4 configuration) and speaks in the bundled demo voice. Enroll your own voice from ~3 s of audio with the sample's `conversion/extract_speaker_embedding.py`, then pass `--speaker my_voice.npy`.

## Android app

The same sample ships an Android app (Kotlin, Compiled Model API, CPU) under `compiled_model_api/text_to_speech_lm/kotlin_cpu/android/`: build with Android Studio or `./gradlew :app:installDebug`, then run `./install_to_device.sh` to download the model files from this repository and push them to the device. Device-verified on Pixel 8a. With the reference `mtp_fp32` + `codec_decoder_fp32` graphs: RTF ≈ 6.7. The app auto-selects the fast graphs when present: `mtp_folded_int8` drops the MTP from ≈333 to ≈68 ms/frame (~5×), and the split `codec_partA`/`codec_partB` drops the codec from ≈114 to ≈40 ms/frame (~2.5×). Together the end-to-end **RTF falls to ≈2.06** (~3.2× vs the reference graphs), ASR-lossless.

## Files

| File | Size | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `talker_int4.tflite` | 256 MB | Talker LM (28-layer Qwen3, prefill_32/prefill_128/decode signatures, KV 1024), blockwise-32 OCTAV int4 weights |
| `talker_fp32.tflite` | 1.8 GB | fp32 talker; under greedy decoding it reproduces the PyTorch reference token-for-token |
| `mtp_fp32.tflite` | 440 MB | MTP decode step (5-layer transformer, 17-slot KV cache, 15 lm_heads), invoked 17× per frame — the exact reference graph |
| `mtp_folded_int8.tflite` | 218 MB | **Fast MTP**: all 16 inner steps × 5 layers folded into one graph (in-graph argmax + embedding gather, KV internal), GPTQ dynamic-int8 weights. One invoke per frame; ~5× faster on device. Drop-in replacement for `mtp_fp32.tflite` |
| `codec_decoder_fp32.tflite` | 457 MB | Codec decoder (RVQ + 8-layer transformer + causal ConvNet, 64-frame chunks → 24 kHz PCM) |
| `codec_partA.tflite` / `codec_partB.tflite` | 163 + 294 MB | **Fast codec**: the decoder split at the transformer/convnet boundary. Part A (transformer) runs fp32; Part B (the conv upsampler, ~all the FLOPs) runs with XNNPACK FORCE_FP16 → ~2.5× on device, ASR-identical. Drop-in replacement for `codec_decoder_fp32.tflite` |
| `tokenizer.json` | 11 MB | Qwen2 BPE tokenizer (Python sample / `tokenizers`) |
| `vocab.json`, `merges.txt` | 4.5 MB | Same vocabulary in raw form (used by the Android app's Kotlin tokenizer) |
| `tables/*` | 723 MB | Host-side embedding tables: codec embedding (fp32), 15 MTP embeddings (fp16), text embedding (fp16), text projection MLP (fp32) |
| `voices/demo_speaker.npy` | 4 KB | Demo voice x-vector (enrolled from the official Qwen3-TTS demo clip) |

## Accuracy

- Each graph is numerically verified against the PyTorch reference: talker bit-exact at torch level and correlation 1.0 / top-1 100% as .tflite; MTP 15/15 greedy tokens; codec decoder correlation 1.0 (max abs diff 1.8e-5).
- End to end with `talker_fp32` + greedy: token-for-token identical codes to the reference implementation, waveform correlation 1.000000, ASR round-trip returns the input sentence.
- `talker_int4` (data-free blockwise-32 OCTAV) produces a different but valid sampling trajectory; outputs transcribe identically under ASR round-trip. Channelwise int8/int4 quantization (the tooling default) degenerates on this model family — use blockwise granularity.

## Performance (Apple M4 Max, CPU/XNNPACK)

| Stage | per 80 ms audio frame |
|---|---|
| Talker decode (8 threads) | 45–50 ms |
| MTP inner loop (17 invokes, 1 thread) | ~148 ms |
| Codec decoder (amortized) | ~10 ms |
| Total | ~205 ms → RTF ≈ 2.5 |

The MTP inner loop dominates (a 78M-parameter transformer streams its weights 17 times per frame). `mtp_folded_int8.tflite` folds those 17 invokes into one graph and quantizes it: on the M4 Max the MTP drops to ~41 ms/frame, and on a Pixel 8a from ~333 to ~68 ms/frame. The fold is token-identical to the reference; the dynamic-int8 weights give a different-but-intelligible trajectory (ASR round-trip exact). The codec then dominates, and `codec_partA`/`codec_partB` split it so the conv-heavy back half runs in fp16 (~2.5× on device). Together the end-to-end RTF drops from ≈6.7 to ≈2.06 on a Pixel 8a (≈1.44 on M4 Max), ASR-lossless. Conversion scripts: [`export_mtp_folded.py` / `gptq_mtp_folded.py` / `export_codec_split.py`](https://github.com/john-rocky/hf-to-litertlm/tree/main/qwen3tts_work). Remaining lever: the talker (now ~52 ms/frame).

### Android (Pixel 8a)

Android figures use the standard TFLite [`benchmark_model`](https://ai.google.dev/edge/litert/models/measurement) on a **Pixel 8a** (Tensor G3, Android 16) — 5 warm-up runs then 20 timed runs, CPU at 4 threads.

| Graph | GPU (OpenCL) | CPU (XNNPACK, 4 threads) |
|---|---|---|
| `mtp_folded_int8.tflite` | 225 ms | 153 ms |
| `mtp_fp32.tflite` | 113 ms | 27 ms |

Nothing here is faster on the GPU; run this pipeline on the CPU on Android.

## Limitations

- Voice cloning is x-vector mode only (speaker embedding). ICL-mode cloning (reference transcript + codec encoding of the reference audio) additionally needs the codec encoder, which is kept off-device (enrollment-time PyTorch).
- The prompt prefill is capped at 32 positions (the x-vector prompt is always 10); the KV cache is 1024 (~80 s of audio), generation is capped at 512 frames (~41 s) in the sample.
- Streaming synthesis (the model's dual-track design supports it) is not implemented in the sample loop yet.

## License

# Bhasani-v0.1: Expressive Neural TTS for Hindi & English (with EmoSteer)

**Bhasani-v0.1** is a high-efficiency neural Text-to-Speech system for **Hindi** and **English**, featuring expressive **emotion steering** via representation hooks without changing base model weights.

This repository bundles:
- **Base Neural Model**: `config.yaml`, `model.safetensors`, `tokenizer.model`
- **Hindi EmoSteer Checkpoint**: `emosteer_hindi.pt`
- **English EmoSteer Checkpoint**: `emosteer_english.pt`
- **Reference Voice Prompts**: `samples/voice_01_f.wav` ... `samples/voice_10_m.wav`
- **Testing Script**: `test_emotions.py`
- **Comprehensive Benchmark Report**: [BENCHMARK_REPORT.md](BENCHMARK_REPORT.md)

**Supported Emotional Conditions:**
`happy` · `sad` · `anger` · `fear` · `disgust` · `surprise` (plus `neutral` baseline)

---

## 1. Installation

```bash
pip install pocket-tts torch soundfile huggingface_hub
```

---

## 2. Quick CLI Testing with `test_emotions.py`

Download `test_emotions.py` from this repository to test speech and emotion generation immediately:

```bash
# Download test runner
wget https://huggingface.co/MindMapDigital/Bhasani-v0.1/raw/main/test_emotions.py

# Test all Hindi emotions (neutral, happy, sad, anger, fear, disgust, surprise)
python test_emotions.py --lang hindi

# Test all English emotions
python test_emotions.py --lang english

# Test a specific emotion with custom text & strength
python test_emotions.py --lang hindi --emotion happy --alpha 2.5 --text "आज का दिन सचमुच बहुत शानदार है!"

# Test English with custom voice prompt or emotion
python test_emotions.py --lang english --emotion surprise --alpha 2.0
```

Generated audio outputs will be saved automatically to `./outputs/`.

---

## 3. Minimal Python Snippet: Hindi Emotion Testing

Copy and run this self-contained script:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import soundfile as sf
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from pocket_tts import TTSModel

REPO = "MindMapDigital/Bhasani-v0.1"
DEVICE = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"

# 1. Load Hindi Base Model (eos_threshold=-1.0 for proper EOS termination)
model = TTSModel.load_model(config=f"hf://{REPO}/config.yaml", eos_threshold=-1.0)
model.to(DEVICE)

# 2. Define and Load EmoSteer Adapter
class EmoSteer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim, num_emotions, eps):
        super().__init__()
        self.We = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(num_emotions, dim, dim) * 0.01)
        self.eps = eps

    def forward(self, z, emotion_ids, alpha):
        we = self.We[emotion_ids]
        v = torch.einsum("btd,bde->bte", z, we)
        return z + alpha * self.eps * v

ckpt_path = hf_hub_download(repo_id=REPO, filename="emosteer_hindi.pt")
ckpt = torch.load(ckpt_path, map_location=DEVICE, weights_only=False)
emotions = ckpt["emotions"]  # ['anger', 'disgust', 'fear', 'happy', 'sad', 'surprise']
d_model = ckpt["state_dict"]["We"].shape[-1]

emo_steer = EmoSteer(d_model, len(emotions), ckpt["eps"]).to(DEVICE)
emo_steer.load_state_dict(ckpt["state_dict"])
emo_steer.eval()

# 3. Speaker reference audio (bundled sample or your own 3-10s WAV)
VOICE_PROMPT = f"hf://{REPO}/samples/voice_01_f.wav"  # or "path/to/your_speaker.wav"
state = model.get_state_for_audio_prompt(VOICE_PROMPT)

# 4. Text to synthesize
TEXT = "आज का दिन बहुत ही खास है। हम सब मिलकर कुछ नया सीखेंगे और आगे बढ़ेंगे।"

# 5. Baseline (Neutral)
audio_neutral = model.generate_audio(state, TEXT)
sf.write("hindi_neutral.wav", audio_neutral.cpu().numpy(), model.sample_rate)
print("Saved -> hindi_neutral.wav")

# 6. Generate Emotional Speech with Forward Hook
ALPHA = 2.0  # steering strength (1.0 = subtle, 2.0 = clear, 3.0 = strong)

for emotion in emotions:
    emotion_id = torch.tensor([emotions.index(emotion)], device=DEVICE)

    def steer_hook(module, input, output):
        return emo_steer(output, emotion_id, ALPHA)

    hook = model.flow_lm.out_norm.register_forward_hook(steer_hook)
    audio = model.generate_audio(state, TEXT)
    hook.remove()  # always remove hook after generation

    out_file = f"hindi_{emotion}.wav"
    sf.write(out_file, audio.cpu().numpy(), model.sample_rate)
    print(f"Saved -> {out_file}")
```

---

## 4. Minimal Python Snippet: English Emotion Testing

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import soundfile as sf
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from pocket_tts import TTSModel

REPO = "MindMapDigital/Bhasani-v0.1"
DEVICE = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"

# 1. Load English Base Model
model = TTSModel.load_model(language="english")
model.to(DEVICE)

# 2. Define and Load English EmoSteer Adapter
class EmoSteer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim, num_emotions, eps):
        super().__init__()
        self.We = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(num_emotions, dim, dim) * 0.01)
        self.eps = eps

    def forward(self, z, emotion_ids, alpha):
        we = self.We[emotion_ids]
        v = torch.einsum("btd,bde->bte", z, we)
        return z + alpha * self.eps * v

ckpt_path = hf_hub_download(repo_id=REPO, filename="emosteer_english.pt")
ckpt = torch.load(ckpt_path, map_location=DEVICE, weights_only=False)
emotions = ckpt["emotions"]
d_model = ckpt["state_dict"]["We"].shape[-1]

emo_steer = EmoSteer(d_model, len(emotions), ckpt["eps"]).to(DEVICE)
emo_steer.load_state_dict(ckpt["state_dict"])
emo_steer.eval()

# 3. Speaker prompt: built-in voice 'alba' or your own WAV file
state = model.get_state_for_audio_prompt("alba")  # or "path/to/reference.wav"

# 4. Text to synthesize
TEXT = "Today is a wonderful day. Let us make the most of every moment we have together."

# 5. Baseline (Neutral)
audio_neutral = model.generate_audio(state, TEXT)
sf.write("english_neutral.wav", audio_neutral.cpu().numpy(), model.sample_rate)
print("Saved -> english_neutral.wav")

# 6. Generate Emotional Speech with Hook
ALPHA = 2.0

for emotion in emotions:
    emotion_id = torch.tensor([emotions.index(emotion)], device=DEVICE)

    def steer_hook(module, input, output):
        return emo_steer(output, emotion_id, ALPHA)

    hook = model.flow_lm.out_norm.register_forward_hook(steer_hook)
    audio = model.generate_audio(state, TEXT)
    hook.remove()

    out_file = f"english_{emotion}.wav"
    sf.write(out_file, audio.cpu().numpy(), model.sample_rate)
    print(f"Saved -> {out_file}")
```

---

## 5. Alpha (Steering Strength) Guide

| `alpha` | Effect | Recommended Use |
|---|---|---|
| **1.0** | Subtle | Slight coloring of tone, highly natural |
| **1.5 - 2.0** | Clear | **Recommended starting point**; distinct emotion while preserving voice fidelity |
| **2.5 - 3.0** | Pronounced | Strong emotional delivery |
| **> 3.5** | Extreme | High expressiveness; may introduce minor saturation |

---

## 6. How EmoSteer Works

EmoSteer applies representation steering directly to the transformer's latent activation space without fine-tuning the base model:

$$\mathbf{z}_{\text{out}} = \mathbf{z} + \alpha \cdot \epsilon \cdot \mathbf{z} \mathbf{W}_e[\text{emotion\_id}]$$

1. A lightweight PyTorch forward hook attaches to `model.flow_lm.out_norm`.
2. During iterative flow matching generation, output latents are steered along the emotion direction matrix $\mathbf{W}_e$.
3. The hook is removed after generation, immediately restoring the base model to neutral state.

---

## 7. Checkpoint Format

The emotion adapter `.pt` files contain:

```python
{
    "state_dict": {
        "We": torch.Tensor  # shape: [num_emotions, 1024, 1024]
    },
    "emotions": ["anger", "disgust", "fear", "happy", "sad", "surprise"],
    "eps": 0.001
}
```

# Pocket-TTS 中英双语 · 拼音版 · AX650 推理包

[Pocket-TTS 中英双语社区版（拼音版）](https://www.tulingyun.com/tts_clone.html)（Mimi 编解码器 + FlowLM/LSD，零样本声音克隆，
**中文按带声调拼音建模，多音字更准**）在 **AX650N** 上的板端推理包：
axmodel + int8 ONNX + Python 运行时 + 音色/词表资源，**即取即用**。

> 交付文件只有 **int8 ONNX**（供应商动态量化），本包把其中的 FlowLM 保留在 CPU int8、
> 将 float 的 `flow_net`/`mimi 卷积` 编译为 axmodel，构成混合 NPU/CPU 推理。

## 实测指标（AX650N，参考音色 Vivian）

| 项目 | Python 运行时 | **C++ 运行时（推荐）** |
|---|---|---|
| 平均 RTF（benchmark 4 数据集） | 0.783 → **0.699**（int8 mimi_tf） | — |
| zh_long | 0.687（int8 mimi_tf） | **0.40~0.44** |
| zh_short | 0.767（aishell3 均长 1.25s 口径） | **0.41~0.42** |
| 首帧延迟（含音色编码+prefill） | 205 ms | **133~146 ms** |
| 相对基线（fp32 mimi_tf） | **-10~11%**（mimi_tf 22→15.5ms/帧） | AR 融合再 -7%（AR 32.8→30.3ms） |
| 回环 CER（SenseVoiceSmall） | 常规中英文本 **0%**；多音字 0%；绕口令 25%（ASR 极限） |
| 对照：vendor int8（主机 CPU） | RTF ≈0.20，同文本 CER 一致或略差 |

逐条指标（RTF/首帧/CER）与机器可读数据：**`metrics.json`**、**`metrics_CER.tsv`**。

### 统一 benchmark（Voice_Test.AXERA）

| 数据集 | 指标 | 数值 | ASR 地板 | 热启动 RTF |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| aishell3（200 条，zh） | 回环 CER | 12.45% | 2.90% | 0.7631 |

## C++ 运行时（推荐，更快）

包内自带 aarch64 预编译二进制（`cpp/bin/`，含 ORT 1.23 运行库，免编译）：
主线程 Flow-AR+flow_net ∥ worker 线程 Mimi 解码（跨帧流水线），并把每层注意力
融合为单个 opset-23 `Attention` 算子（674→518 节点，数值等价）。

```bash
# 主机侧分词（与板端前端一致）
python3 tools/prepare_tokens.py --text "你好，世界。" --out req.tokens
# 板端
TOKENS_FILE=cpp/req/zh_short.tokens bash cpp/run_cpp.sh out.wav
```

实测（AX650N，融合 AR + int8 mimi_tf）：**zh_short RTF ≈0.41~0.42 / zh_long ≈0.40~0.44**，首帧 133~146ms，回环 CER 0%。
（Python 版 benchmark 均 RTF 0.70；C++ 相对 Python 提速约 1.7x。）

## 板端运行

环境：AX650N（BSP + `axengine` wheel + `onnxruntime` + `numpy/soundfile/scipy/sentencepiece/pypinyin`），Python 3.10+。

```bash

bash run_ax650.sh "你好，世界。"

# 长文本（自动分块 + 块间 120ms）
TEXT_FILE=long.txt bash run_ax650.sh

# 批量（载入一次跑多条，RTF 口径同 benchmark）
python3 board/pocket_tts_batch.py --texts-json configs/listen_texts.json \
  --out-dir output --onnx-dir models --axmodel-dir models --cpu-model-dir models/cpu \
  --mimi-split-dir models/mimi_split --tokens-txt models/tokens.txt \
  --bpe-model models/chn_jpn_yue_eng_ko_spectok.bpe.model --reference models/Vivian.wav \
  --threads 4 --prefill-threads 8 --flow-ar-model flow_ar_step.onnx \
  --flow-prefill-model flow_step_windowed.onnx --mimi-tf-model mimi_transformer_step.onnx \
  --encoder-dir models/encoder --flow-net-model flow_net_step_fp32.axmodel \
  --mimi-conv-model mimi_conv_step.axmodel
```

把 `--npu-flow-net` 改为 `0`（脚本会读取 `models/cpu/flow_net_step.onnx`）。

1. 阿拉伯数字 → 中文（2026→二零二六，-3.5→负三点五；本项目增强）；

# krapas-Regina 🌿 — Lithuanian TTS voice (OmniVoice fine-tune)

A Lithuanian text-to-speech voice: [OmniVoice](https://github.com/k2-fsa/OmniVoice)
(k2-fsa, 0.6 B) fine-tuned on **3.05 hours** of read Lithuanian speech from a single
female speaker recorded for the LIEPA **speech-synthesis** project (Regina Jokubauskaitė). Runs on a Mac (MPS), an NVIDIA GPU, or CPU —
nothing leaves the machine.

Listen first: [**sudi.lt/balsas**](https://sudi.lt/balsas/) — this checkpoint next to
a second voice and to ElevenLabs v3 on the same sentences (homographs, nasal vowels,
numbers, abbreviations, foreign names).

Vegetable-garden lineage of open Lithuanian speech models:
svogūnas 🧅 → paprika 🌶️ (ASR) → bananas 🍌 (stress) → kmynas 🌱 (ASR) → krapas 🌿 (voice).

## The part that matters for Lithuanian: stress marks in, not plain text

Lithuanian does not write stress, but stress decides pronunciation and meaning —
*kãsa* (a braid) vs *kasà* (a till), *mãno* vs *màno*, *sū́nus* vs *sūnùs*. A model that
sees only letters guesses, and guesses wrong often enough to be noticed.

So this model was trained on **stress-marked text**, and expects stress-marked text at
inference. Two steps run before it:

1. **Normalisation** — digits, dates, times, units, abbreviations and initials become
   words in the right case. The model has never seen a digit and never will.
2. **Stress marking** — [`kristijonas/banano-kirtis-v2`](https://huggingface.co/kristijonas/banano-kirtis-v2)
   (try it at [bananas.sudi.lt](https://bananas.sudi.lt)) puts the marks on, in context.

Feed it unmarked text and it still speaks, but the stress becomes a lottery.
Almost every stress error you hear is the stresser's, not the voice's — which is good
news, because a wrong word in a dictionary is a one-line fix, not a retrain.

## Usage

```python
import torch
from omnivoice import OmniVoice, OmniVoiceGenerationConfig

m = OmniVoice.from_pretrained("kristijonas/krapas-Regina",
                              device_map="mps", dtype=torch.float32)   # "cuda" / "cpu" also fine
cfg = OmniVoiceGenerationConfig(guidance_scale=4, num_step=32)

wav = m.generate(text="Šiuõ metù galiù pažiūrė́ti pro lángą mán iš dešinė̃s mataũ spar̃ną.",
                 language="lt", generation_config=cfg, normalize_text=False)[0]

import soundfile as sf
sf.write("out.wav", wav, 24000)
```

Three settings that decide the result:

- **`guidance_scale=4`** (the library default is 2). At 2 the model skips part of the
  stress marks; at 4 it follows the text. This is the single most important knob.
- **`num_step=32`**. 16 is roughly twice as fast with visibly more artefacts.
- **`normalize_text=False`** — the built-in normaliser does not know Lithuanian; do the
  normalising yourself before the stresser (see above).

**Unicode form matters.** Train and inference text must carry the same combining marks:
NFC for the letters, the combining accents (U+0300 grave, U+0301 acute, U+0303 tilde)
left as separate code points. If you feed fully-composed or fully-decomposed text, part
of the marks stop being seen.

**One sentence at a time.** The training clips are short (mean 2.1 s, longest 5.1 s), so
generate sentence by sentence and join with silence — 0.4 s between sentences, 0.9 s
between paragraphs. A single request over ~15 s degrades.

Output is 24 kHz mono. On an M-series Mac a minute of speech takes about 1.3 minutes to
generate; on an NVIDIA GPU it is faster than realtime.

## Data

| | |
|---|---|
| Source | [`meldynamics/liepa-tts`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/meldynamics/liepa-tts) — utterance-level audio recorded for the LIEPA speech-synthesis project, Vilnius University, CC BY 4.0. Not LIEPA-3, which is the ASR corpus |
| Speaker | Regina Jokubauskaitė, read speech, studio |
| Clips | 5,124 (5,024 train / 100 dev), **3.05 h**, mean 2.14 s, range 0.17–5.14 s |
| Text | stress-marked: 4,891 clips human-marked, 233 from an engine fallback |
| Punctuation | LIEPA transcripts carry none; a terminal `.` was appended to every line |

Because the transcripts have no internal punctuation, the model learned sentence-final
intonation from that appended period and little else. Questions and exclamations are
weaker than in a voice recorded from punctuated script.

## Training

```json
{
  "init_from_checkpoint": "k2-fsa/OmniVoice",
  "learning_rate": 1e-5,
  "batch_tokens": 8192,
  "prompt_ratio_range": [0.0, 0.3],
  "steps": 5000,
  "save_steps": 500,
  "mixed_precision": "bf16",
  "weight_decay": 0.01,
  "warmup_ratio": 0.01,
  "seed": 42
}
```

One A100 80 GB, ~35 minutes including audio tokenisation. This is **checkpoint 5000**,
picked by listening to 1000 / 2500 / 5000 — not by a metric. With 5 k clips there is no
eval number that tells you which checkpoint sounds better; listen.

The repo bundles OmniVoice's `audio_tokenizer/`, so `from_pretrained` works on its own
without the base snapshot.

## What it does not do

- **Digits, dates, units** — the normaliser's job, not the model's.
- **Foreign names it has not seen** — it reads them as Lithuanian letters.
- **Emotion** — the data is calm read speech; that is what comes out.
- **Whispering, singing, speaker mixing** — no.
- Each generation differs slightly from the last; the same sentence twice is not the same
  waveform.

## Ethics

This is a real person's voice, released as part of a corpus published under CC BY 4.0 for
speech technology. Attribution to LIEPA / Vilnius University is required, and the voice
should not be used to make that person appear to say things she did not say —
endorsements, statements, or anything presented as a recording of her.

The same technology suits telephone fraud: a call in a familiar voice is no longer
science fiction. Agree with your family on how you verify who is calling.

## Licence

- Weights: **CC BY-NC 4.0** — OmniVoice's weights are CC BY-NC, and this derivative
  inherits that. Personal and non-commercial use only.
- OmniVoice code: Apache 2.0.
- Training data: the LIEPA speech-synthesis recordings via `meldynamics/liepa-tts`, CC BY 4.0 (Vilnius University).
- A commercial Lithuanian voice needs a base with an Apache/MIT licence, trained from
  scratch on LIEPA — a different project.

## Guide

The whole path — which sentences to record, how to record so the model does not learn
your breathing, how to check and trim the takes, the training config, and how to wire up
the stresser — is written up in Lithuanian:
[sudi.lt/gidai/savo-balsas](https://sudi.lt/gidai/savo-balsas).

Stressing the text before the voice model was [Mindaugas Žvirblis](https://github.com/blinkinglight)'s idea: 32 letters are
too few for a voice, and marking stress turns them into ~80 distinct sounds.

# Magpie-TTS Saudi Voice Clone

Zero-shot voice-cloning text-to-speech for **Saudi Arabic**, with Modern Standard Arabic and English retained from the base model. Fine-tuned by IST Networks from NVIDIA's `magpie_tts_multilingual_357m`.

Give it a 3 to 10 second clip of any speaker and a sentence; it speaks the sentence in that voice. There are no built-in speakers: the reference clip is required for every request.

| | |
|---|---|
| Released checkpoint | step 78 000, epoch 38 of 40 (lowest validation loss) |
| Validation loss | 10.219 (started at 11.276) |
| Output | 22.05 kHz mono, via NeMo NanoCodec |
| Parameters | 357 M (339 M pretrained + 18 M context encoder trained from scratch) |
| Framework | NeMo Speech toolkit, commit `ca3f93a5` |

Listen to `samples/` before integrating. `ar-SA_*.wav` are Saudi sentences, `en_*.wav` are one English sentence spoken through Saudi and English voices.

## Contents

```
magpie_tts_saudi_step78000.nemo        fine-tuned model (1.5 GB)
codec/nemo-nano-codec-22khz-*.nemo     audio codec required at inference (425 MB)
inference.py                           CLI + Python API, single sentence or batch
voices/                                reference clips: male_saudi, female_saudi, adnan, aria_en, sofia_en
samples/                               outputs from this checkpoint
training/                              the fine-tuning recipe (config, launcher, data scripts, logs)
```

## Quick start

### Environment

Tested with Python 3.11, PyTorch 2.11 (CUDA 12.9), NVIDIA RTX A6000. The Magpie-TTS inference modules live in the NeMo Speech repository, pinned to the commit the model was trained with.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech.git
cd Speech && git checkout ca3f93a516ff172e32951928aea6f96a977a7600
pip install -e ".[tts]"
pip install soundfile huggingface_hub
```

Alternatively, the NVIDIA NeMo container `nvcr.io/nvidia/nemo:25.xx` with the repository above checked out on top works the same way.

### Download

```bash
hf download ISTNetworks/magpie --local-dir magpie-tts-saudi
cd magpie-tts-saudi
```

### Speak one sentence

```bash
python inference.py \
  --text "هلا والله، كيف الحال؟ اليوم الجو حلو مرة." \
  --ref voices/male_saudi.wav --lang ar-SA --out hello.wav
```

English in the same voice:

```bash
python inference.py --text "Good morning, and thank you for joining us." \
  --ref voices/male_saudi.wav --lang en --out hello_en.wav
```

### Batch

One request per line in a JSONL file:

```json
{"text": "أبشر، بكرة أرسل لك كل التفاصيل.", "context_audio_filepath": "voices/female_saudi.wav", "language": "ar-SA", "name": "greeting_01"}
{"text": "Your order has shipped.", "context_audio_filepath": "voices/adnan.wav", "language": "en", "name": "order_en"}
```

```bash
python inference.py --manifest requests.jsonl --out_dir outputs/
```

### Python API (for a service)

```python
from inference import MagpieTTS

tts = MagpieTTS("magpie_tts_saudi_step78000.nemo",
                "codec/nemo-nano-codec-22khz-1.89kbps-21.5fps.nemo")   # load once, ~40 s

wav, sr = tts.synthesize("النص هنا", ref_wav="voices/female_saudi.wav", lang="ar-SA")
# wav: float32 numpy array, sr: 22050
```

`synthesize_batch([...])` takes a list of `Request(text, ref_wav, lang)` and runs them in one GPU pass. Requests with different languages are grouped automatically.

### Languages

| `--lang` | tokenizer | trained on |
|---|---|---|
| `ar-SA` | Arabic character tokenizer | Saudi dialect speech (18.6 h) |
| `ar` | Arabic character tokenizer | Modern Standard Arabic, with and without diacritics (5 h) |
| `en` | English IPA phoneme tokenizer | GLOBE English (2 h) plus the base model's pretraining |

Dialect comes from the reference voice, not from the language code. `ar-SA` and `ar` use the same character set; the distinction exists so you can pass MSA text with diacritics when you have them.

### Reference clip rules

- 3 to 10 seconds. Shorter clips are rejected; longer ones are cut to the first 10 seconds.
- One speaker, clean speech, no music or crosstalk. 6 to 9 seconds of natural sentences works best.
- Mono 22.05 kHz WAV is what training used. Other rates are resampled on load.
- The clip's language does not need to match the text. Saudi reference with English text works, see `samples/en_*.wav`.

### Sampling parameters

Defaults match the released samples: temperature 0.6, top-k 80, classifier-free guidance scale 2.5. Lower temperature (0.4 to 0.5) is more stable for long production text; `--no_cfg` roughly halves latency at a quality cost.

Performance on one RTX A6000: model load about 40 s; a batch of 3 sentences of 5 to 10 s each synthesizes in 3 to 7 s after warm-up, roughly real-time factor 0.3.

## Known limitations

- **Digits and symbols are dropped in Arabic.** The Arabic character tokenizer has no entries for `0-9`, `٠-٩`, `%`, or the tatweel `ـ`. A sentence containing "30 ألف" is spoken as "ألف". Convert numbers to words before synthesis. English text is unaffected; the phoneme tokenizer normalizes digits.
- Long paragraphs are split into sentences internally. Prosody across sentence boundaries is not modeled, so for voice-over work, synthesize sentence by sentence and concatenate.
- Voice similarity for speakers far from the training distribution (children, heavily processed audio) has not been evaluated.
- `MagpieTTSModel.do_tts()` from the base model does not work with this checkpoint. It relies on the baked speaker table that was removed. Use `inference.py` or the manifest-driven `examples/tts/magpietts_inference.py`.

## Building a production container

Sketch of what a Dockerfile needs, in order:

1. Base image with CUDA 12.x and Python 3.11, or `nvcr.io/nvidia/nemo`.
2. Clone the NeMo Speech repository at commit `ca3f93a5` and `pip install -e ".[tts]"`.
3. Copy this repository's `*.nemo`, `codec/`, `voices/`, and `inference.py` into the image, or mount them as a volume.
4. Set `TORCH_FORCE_NO_WEIGHTS_ONLY_LOAD=1` in the environment. `inference.py` also sets it, but a server entrypoint that imports NeMo before `inference.py` needs it earlier.
5. Wrap `MagpieTTS` in your HTTP layer. Load the model once at startup; the class is not thread-safe, so serialize calls or run one worker per GPU.

The `.nemo` archive contains the model config and weights; the codec is loaded separately, which is why `inference.py` takes both paths.

## Fine-tuning recipe

Everything needed to reproduce or continue training is in `training/`.

### Starting point

`nvidia/magpie_tts_multilingual_357m` (v2607) ships five baked-in English voices and, because of that table, never trains its context encoder. Two preparation steps unlock cloning:

1. `strip_baked.py` removes the baked speaker table from the checkpoint. With it gone, the model uses reference audio for speaker identity.
2. `inject_ctx_encoder.py` writes freshly initialized weights for the 18 M-parameter context encoder, whose tensors the loader requires.

### Data

| set | utterances | hours | tokenizer | weight |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Saudi male (multi-speaker) | 5 084 | 8.0 | ar-SA chars | 1.5 |
| Saudi female (multi-speaker) | 4 535 | 4.4 | ar-SA chars | 1.2 |
| Adnan (single speaker) | 2 940 | 6.1 | ar-SA chars | 0.6 |
| ClArTTS, MSA with diacritics | 2 153 | 2.5 | ar-MSA chars | 0.9 |
| ClArTTS, diacritics stripped | 2 153 | 2.5 | ar-MSA chars | 0.9 |
| GLOBE English | 2 138 | 2.1 | English phonemes | 1.3 |

`build_manifests.py` pairs each utterance with a same-speaker reference clip (3 to 10 s), holds out 5 male and 3 female speakers entirely for cloning evaluation, and creates the undiacritized ClArTTS twin so the model learns both surface forms. Manifest lines carry `context_audio_filepath` and never `context_text`; a populated `context_text` would silently replace the reference audio and the encoder would not train. `manifest_example.jsonl` shows the shape.

### Training

`train_launcher.py` wraps the stock `examples/tts/magpietts.py` flow with two additions: a separate learning rate for the context encoder, and a gradient probe that logs the encoder's gradient norm so a silent "encoder never trains" failure is caught on step 0.

| | |
|---|---|
| Optimizer | AdamW, lr 5e-6 for pretrained weights, 1e-4 for the context encoder |
| Batch | 8, precision fp32, gradient clip 2.5 |
| Schedule | 40 epochs × 2 000 weighted-sampling steps, 80 000 steps total |
| Hardware | 1 × RTX A6000 48 GB, 32.7 GB used, about 36 min per epoch, 24 h total |
| Checkpointing | every epoch on `val_loss`, top 5 kept |
| Early stopping | patience 10 epochs, never triggered |

Run order: `run_smoke.sh` (3 steps, asserts nonzero encoder gradient) then `gate_and_train.sh`, which starts `run_train.sh` only if the smoke test passed. `gate.log` records the gate decision for this run.

### Validation loss

Full history in `val_loss_history.csv`; the complete training log is `train.log.gz`.

| epoch | 0 | 4 | 9 | 14 | 19 | 24 | 29 | 34 | 38 | 39 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| val_loss | 11.276 | 10.666 | 10.464 | 10.377 | 10.316 | 10.284 | 10.251 | 10.236 | **10.219** | 10.225 |

Train loss at the end was 9.7, a 0.5 gap to validation, so mild overfitting had begun but was not yet audible. The curve was flat from epoch 33 onward; a longer run at this learning rate would not help. More Saudi data, or number verbalization in the text, is the next lever.

### Export

`export_nemo.py` loads a Lightning `.ckpt` with its `hparams.yaml` and saves a standalone `.nemo`. `hparams_step78000.yaml` is the config the released checkpoint was trained with.

## License

The base model and codec are released by NVIDIA under the [NVIDIA Open Model License](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/agreements/enterprise-software/nvidia-open-model-license). This fine-tune inherits those terms. The Saudi speech data used for fine-tuning is proprietary to IST Networks and is not included; the five clips in `voices/` are provided only as reference-voice examples for inference.

# Atomtan Studio LoRA Library

A growing library of LoRAs by **Atomtan Studio**, with downloads, trigger words, settings, and compatibility notes together on one page.

The first release is **DreamPop v2 for YuE2-3B**, a music style adapter intended for atmospheric dream pop. More adapters can be added to this same repository, organized by base model and style.

## Available LoRAs

| LoRA | Base model | Checkpoint | Trigger | Download |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **DreamPop v2** | YuE2-3B | 1,000 steps | `sv_dreampop` | [dreampop_sv_dreampop.safetensors](https://huggingface.co/atomtanstudio/lora-library/resolve/main/yue2/dreampop/dreampop_sv_dreampop.safetensors?download=true) |

## DreamPop v2

DreamPop v2 was trained from fresh adapters on 32 reviewed recordings across 12 artists, using the FL YuE2 `native_joint_v1` training recipe. It trains both the autoregressive (AR) and acoustic (NAR) components of YuE2. This release contains the final **1,000-step checkpoint** in a single combined export for Sound & Vision.

This is an adapter, not a standalone music model. Download and install the base model separately: [m-a-p/YuE2-3B](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/YuE2-3B).

### Trigger and starting settings

Use **`sv_dreampop`** in the style prompt. For example:

```text
sv_dreampop, dream pop, shimmering guitars, soft vocals, spacious reverb, steady mid-tempo drums
```

| Setting | Starting value |
| --- | --- |
| LoRA strength | `1.0` |
| Symbolic planning / CoT | `off` |
| Guidance / CFG | `1.0` |
| Acoustic synthesis steps | `32` |
| Inference engine | Native YuE2 BF16 |

Use your own lyrics and adjust the musical description for the song. These settings are a starting point, not a claim that one setting or checkpoint is best for every prompt.

### Install in Sound & Vision

Use [Sound & Vision](https://github.com/atomtanstudio/sound-and-vision) with support for native YuE2 LoRA exports, available in commit [`440e4ee`](https://github.com/atomtanstudio/sound-and-vision/commit/440e4eed0391d94700f84e843669289cf7ec5cf2).

1. Download the checkpoint above and the accompanying [lora.json](https://huggingface.co/atomtanstudio/lora-library/resolve/main/yue2/dreampop/lora.json?download=true).
2. Place both files on the computer running the backend, under `<app>/loras/styles/DreamPop-v2/`.
3. Refresh the app or rescan the LoRA folder, then select **DreamPop v2** and **Step 1,000** under **Trained styles & artists**.
4. Start with strength `1.0`. Sound & Vision reads the trigger and generation defaults from the sidecar and checkpoint metadata.

If `SOUND_VISION_LORAS` points to a custom directory, use that directory instead of `<app>/loras`.

### Format and compatibility

The uploaded file uses **`sound-vision-yue2-native-export-v1`**. It combines the original AR and NAR adapter pair into fused projections while preserving their tensor values and scaling. Both learned components are included; Sound & Vision does not need a second adapter file for this release.

This is a custom YuE2 adapter layout. The `.safetensors` extension alone does not establish compatibility with other loaders. Direct loading in generic ComfyUI, Diffusers, or PEFT loaders has not been verified. FL YuE2 workflows that expect separate AR and NAR files need the original pair or an appropriate conversion; do not supply this combined file as either member of that pair.

### Training and verification

| Property | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Base-model revision | `1a96eca688d6ae5d7f0feb88573fec89920fcd19` |
| Training recipe | FL YuE2 `native_joint_v1` |
| Training steps | 1,000 |
| LoRA rank | 32 |
| Learning rate | `0.0001`, constant |
| Dataset | 32 recordings across 12 artists |
| Components | AR and NAR |
| Export precision | FP32 |
| Tensor count | 672 |
| File size | 234,969,024 bytes, approximately 235 MB |

The completed run recorded finite losses and active gradients for both components. Export verification checked every source tensor and preserved unit scaling. The downloadable file was checked against the export's SHA-256 digest after renaming.

These are training and file-integrity checks, not a held-out quality benchmark. Training previews used a 120-second diagnostic cap; that cap is not a recommended generation length or evidence that a full song will end naturally. Results vary with lyrics, prompt, seed, and runtime. The 1,000-step checkpoint is the final checkpoint from this run, not an independently established best checkpoint.

### Checksum

```text
617852d379c66b0407879421a353233d29cda8188cca82973a94c61b512ca03d  dreampop_sv_dreampop.safetensors
```

Also available in [SHA256SUMS](https://huggingface.co/atomtanstudio/lora-library/blob/main/SHA256SUMS).


# Orpheus-TTS Conditioned (100k Checkpoint)

Modelo **Orpheus-TTS** ajustado em modo condicionado utilizando o dataset `freds0/TAGARELA_v2`. Este modelo realiza síntese de voz (TTS) Zero-Shot: ele recebe um áudio de referência e o texto que foi dito nele, junto com o novo texto que deve ser gerado, e produz a nova fala seguindo o ritmo e o timbre da voz original.

> **Nota sobre o formato do prompt:** Apenas treinamos o modelo de forma zero-shot mantendo estritamente o formato original do modelo pré-treinado. Ou seja, a entrada consiste apenas em concatenar o texto de referência com o texto a ser gerado, seguidos pelos códigos do áudio de referência codificado (ref codes).

## Como utilizar (Inferência Completa)

Abaixo está o script completo que carrega o modelo, processa um áudio de referência, e possui o loop de *retry* com `repetition_penalty` para lidar com falhas na predição do token `[EOSP]`.

```python
import torch
import torchaudio
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
from snac import SNAC

def get_snac_codes(audio_path, snac_model, device="cuda"):
    audio, sr = torchaudio.load(audio_path)
    if audio.shape[0] > 1:
        audio = audio.mean(dim=0, keepdim=True)
    if sr != snac_model.sample_rate:
        audio = torchaudio.functional.resample(audio, sr, snac_model.sample_rate)
    audio = audio.unsqueeze(0).to(device)
    with torch.no_grad():
        codes = snac_model.encode(audio)
    
    # Flatten the hierarchical codes
    code_list = []
    for i in range(codes[0].shape[-1]):
        code_list.append(codes[0][0, i].item())
        code_list.extend(codes[1][0, 2*i:2*i+2].tolist())
        code_list.extend(codes[2][0, 4*i:4*i+4].tolist())
    return code_list

def redistribute_codes(codes):
    """Reconstruct the hierarchical SNAC structure."""
    c1, c2, c3 = [], [], []
    i = 0
    while i < len(codes):
        c1.append(codes[i]); i += 1
        if i < len(codes): c2.extend(codes[i:i+2]); i += 2
        if i < len(codes): c3.extend(codes[i:i+4]); i += 4
    return [
        torch.tensor([c1], dtype=torch.long),
        torch.tensor([c2], dtype=torch.long),
        torch.tensor([c3], dtype=torch.long)
    ]

# 1. Carregar os modelos
device = "cuda"
model_path = "lgris/orpheus-tts-zeroshot-tagarela_v2"

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_path, torch_dtype=torch.float16).to(device)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_path)
snac_model = SNAC.from_pretrained("hubertsiuzdak/snac_24khz").to(device).eval()

# IDs Especiais
start_of_human = 128259
end_of_human = 128260
start_of_ai = 128261
start_of_speech = 128257
end_of_speech = 128258
start_of_text = 128000
end_of_text = 128009
base_offset = 128266

# 2. Preparar os inputs
ref_text = "Texto falado no áudio de referência."
target_text = "Texto que você deseja gerar."
ref_audio_path = "referencia.wav"

text_ids = tokenizer.encode(f"{ref_text} {target_text}", add_special_tokens=False)
ref_codes = [c + base_offset for c in get_snac_codes(ref_audio_path, snac_model, device)]

input_ids = (
    [start_of_human, start_of_text] + text_ids + [end_of_text, end_of_human] +
    [start_of_ai, start_of_speech] + ref_codes
)
input_tensor = torch.tensor([input_ids], dtype=torch.long, device=device)

# 3. Loop de Geração (Retry se não houver EOS)
max_retries = 3
final_audio = None

for attempt in range(max_retries):
    with torch.no_grad():
        output = model.generate(
            input_tensor,
            max_new_tokens=1500,
            do_sample=True,
            temperature=0.7,
            top_p=0.95,
            repetition_penalty=1.2, # Penaliza tokens de silêncio para forçar término
            pad_token_id=tokenizer.pad_token_id,
            eos_token_id=end_of_speech,
            min_new_tokens=50,
        )
    
    generated = output[0].tolist()
    generated_codes = generated[len(input_ids):]
    
    if end_of_speech in generated_codes:
        generated_codes = generated_codes[:generated_codes.index(end_of_speech)]
        
        # Decodificar o áudio gerado
        decoded_codes = [c - base_offset for c in generated_codes]
        hierarchical_codes = redistribute_codes(decoded_codes)
        hierarchical_codes = [c.to(device) for c in hierarchical_codes]
        
        with torch.no_grad():
            final_audio = snac_model.decode(hierarchical_codes)
        print("Geração concluída com sucesso!")
        break
    else:
        print(f"Tentativa {attempt + 1}: Modelo não gerou o EOS. Tentando novamente...")

if final_audio is not None:
    torchaudio.save("output.wav", final_audio.cpu().squeeze(0), 24000)
else:
    print("Falha na geração (EOS não encontrado após múltiplas tentativas).")
```
